choosing: Theories of conduct, cultural pluralism, personality, adjustment and the role of home, parents and media repeat across the papers.
Use Indian examples (festivals, family practices, Gandhi, Vivekananda) — they make value-education answers concrete.

topics.name: Home, Parents & Community in Value Development
topics.summary: Home as the first learning place, role of parents, family and community, socialisation, ways to build values at home.
points: Home is the first school: children learn language, habits, manners and values by imitating family members.
Role of parents: role models, set rules and routines, give love and security, encourage honesty and responsibility, discuss right and wrong, praise good behaviour.
Socialisation: the process by which a child learns the norms and values of society. Agencies: family (primary), peers, school, community, media, religion.
Community: festivals, neighbourhood, religious and social groups teach cooperation, respect and service.
Ways to inculcate values at home: storytelling, family rituals and festivals, shared chores, discussing news and dilemmas, consistent discipline, parents practising what they preach.
topics.frame: Meaning → role or ways as headed points with a home example → conclusion.

topics.name: Morality & Theories of Conduct
topics.summary: Facets of morality, the 'good' and self-realisation, rules and theories of conduct.
points: Morality: principles of right and wrong that guide behaviour.
Facets: personal (honesty, self-control), social (justice, respect for others), religious/spiritual, professional.
The 'Good': what is worth pursuing for its own sake; self-realisation: developing one's full potential — the highest good in Indian and idealist ethics.
Rules of conduct: customs, laws, social norms and conscience.

Theories of conduct: hedonism (pleasure is the good — egoistic and altruistic/utilitarian: greatest happiness of the greatest number), rigorism/duty (Kant — act from duty, treat people as ends), perfectionism/self-realisation, intuitionism (conscience knows right), Gita's nishkama karma (action without attachment to results).
topics.frame: Meaning → each theory with its main idea, a thinker and one example → criticism in one line → conclusion.

topics.name: Interaction, Adjustment & Conflict
topics.summary: Verbal and non-verbal interaction, adjustment and its push/pull factors, adjustment disorder, conflict.
points: Verbal interaction: spoken or written words. Non-verbal: gestures, facial expressions, posture, eye contact, tone, touch, space.
Adjustment: the process of balancing one's needs with the demands of the environment.
Push factors (drive a person out of a situation): stress, conflict, failure, rejection. Pull factors (attract towards a new situation): opportunities, acceptance, rewards.
Adjustment disorder: emotional or behavioural symptoms (anxiety, low mood, aggression) after a stressful change.
Helping maladjusted children: counselling, supportive family and teachers, a warm class climate, activities and sports, positive reinforcement, cooperation with parents.
Conflict: a clash of interests, values or needs. Reasons: differences in values and goals, competition for resources, poor communication, personality differences.
topics.frame: Meaning → causes or factors as headed points → remedies → conclusion.

topics.name: Personality & Character
topics.summary: Characteristics of personality, character–personality patterns, personality disorders.
points: Personality: the unique, organised pattern of a person's thoughts, feelings and behaviour.
Characteristics: unique, dynamic, consistent, both inherited and acquired, social, goal-directed.
Character: the moral side of personality — honesty, responsibility, self-control.
Character–personality patterns: amoral, expedient, conforming, irrational-conscientious, rational-altruistic (Peck and Havighurst).
Personality disorders: paranoid, schizoid, antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic, avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive (clusters A, B, C).
topics.frame: Definition → characteristics or types as headed points → conclusion.

topics.name: Indian Culture, Philosophy & Cultural Pluralism
topics.summary: Values of Indian culture, schools of Indian philosophy, cultural pluralism and its challenges.
points: Values of Indian culture: tolerance, non-violence (ahimsa), truth, respect for elders, hospitality, family bonds, spirituality, unity in diversity, 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam'.
Schools of Indian philosophy: orthodox (accept the Vedas) — Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta; heterodox — Charvaka, Buddhism, Jainism.
Cultural pluralism: many cultures, religions and languages living together while keeping their identity (India's unity in diversity).
Challenges: communal tension, regionalism, linguistic conflict, stereotypes, inequality. Response: tolerance, dialogue, constitutional values, education.
topics.frame: Meaning → headed points → Indian examples → conclusion.

topics.name: Value Education: Meaning, Need & Methods
topics.summary: Education and value education, need and importance, moral vs religious education, ways to develop values, malaise of society.
points: Value education: education that develops moral, social, cultural and spiritual values along with knowledge.
Need: moral decline, violence, corruption, consumerism, stress; to build character, responsible citizens and social harmony.
Moral education teaches right conduct based on reason and universal values; religious education teaches the beliefs and practices of a particular religion.
Ways to develop values: school curriculum, teacher as role model, stories and discussions, co-curricular activities, community service, celebrating festivals, value clarification.
Malaise of Indian society: corruption, communalism, casteism, gender discrimination, violence, consumerism, environmental neglect.
topics.frame: Meaning → need or methods as headed points → conclusion.

topics.name: Peers & Media
topics.summary: Value development through peers; role, functions, evolution and negative effects of media.
points: Peers: people of the same age group. They shape values through acceptance, imitation, cooperation and competition — positively (teamwork, sharing) or negatively (peer pressure).
Media: channels of mass communication — print, radio, TV, cinema, internet and social media.
Evolution: print → radio → television → internet → social media and mobile.
Functions: inform, educate, entertain, persuade, shape public opinion, transmit culture.
Negative effects: violence and obscenity, misinformation, addiction and screen time, consumerism, unrealistic body images, cyberbullying.
topics.frame: Meaning → role or effects as headed points → how parents and schools can guide → conclusion.

topics.name: Democracy & Sustainable Development
topics.summary: Principles of democracy, democracy in education, sustainable development and the role of education.
points: Principles of democracy: liberty, equality, fraternity, justice, rule of law, respect for individual dignity.
Democracy in education: equal opportunity, student participation, freedom of expression, respect for differences, cooperative learning.
Sustainable development: meeting present needs without compromising future generations (Brundtland, 1987); economic, social and environmental pillars.
Education for sustainable development: awareness, responsible consumption, conservation habits, values of care for nature.
topics.frame: Meaning → principles or role as headed points → conclusion.
